Recent advancements aim to address this limitation by enabling large language models (LLMs) to generate soft, abstract tokens, thus facilitating reasoning within a continuous concept space. This paper explores the `Soft Thinking' capabilities of various LLMs by examining the models' internal behavior using a suite of probing techniques. Contrary to the common belief that Soft Thinking enables the simultaneous exploration of diverse reasoning paths, our findings reveal that LLMs predominantly rely on the most influential component of the soft inputs during subsequent decoding steps. This reliance hinders the exploration of different reasoning paths and reduces vanilla Soft Thinking to a form of greedy decoding, obscuring the advantage of transmitting more information through Soft Tokens. To tackle this issue, we explore sampling strategies to introduce \emph{randomness}, employing methods such as Dirichlet resampling and the Gumbel-Softmax trick. Our experiments demonstrate that incorporating randomness can alleviate the limitations of vanilla approaches and unleash the potential of Soft Thinking. Notably, the Gumbel-Softmax trick provides adequate randomness with controlled smoothness, resulting in superior performance across eight reasoning benchmarks.

papers.title: Implicit Reasoning in Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Survey
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong generalization across a wide range of tasks. Reasoning with LLMs is central to solving multi-step problems and complex decision-making. To support efficient reasoning, recent studies have shifted attention from explicit chain-of-thought prompting toward implicit reasoning, where reasoning occurs silently via latent structures without emitting intermediate textual steps. Implicit reasoning brings advantages such as lower generation cost, faster inference, and better alignment with internal computation. Although prior surveys have discussed latent representations in the context of reasoning, a dedicated and mechanism-level examination of how reasoning unfolds internally within LLMs remains absent. This survey fills that gap by introducing a taxonomy centered on execution paradigms, shifting the focus from representational forms to computational strategies. We organize existing methods into three execution paradigms based on \textbf{\textit{how and where internal computation unfolds}}: latent optimization, signal-guided control, and layer-recurrent execution. We also review structural, behavioral and representation-based evidence that supports the presence of implicit reasoning in LLMs. We further provide a structured overview of the evaluation metrics and benchmarks used in existing works to assess the effectiveness and reliability of implicit reasoning. We maintain a continuously updated project at: https://github.com/digailab/awesome-llm-implicit-reasoning.

papers.title: Making Natural Language Reasoning Explainable and Faithful
papers.research_question: How to make natural language reasoning explainable and faithful, addressing challenges like inaccurate reasoning and hallucinations in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes leveraging structured semantic graphs for explainable multi-hop question answering and a multi-module interpretable framework for inductive reasoning to improve faithfulness and accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The approaches enhance explainability and faithfulness in natural language reasoning by grounding reasoning in structured information and using modular, iterative processes.
papers.key_findings:
Leveraging semantic graphs in prompting helps models generate higher-quality and more faithful reasoning chains.
The multi-module framework decomposes inductive reasoning into interpretable steps with iterative feedback, reducing hallucinations.
papers.abstract: Neural models, including large language models (LLMs), achieve superior performance on logical reasoning tasks such as question answering. To elicit reasoning capabilities from LLMs, recent works propose using the chain-of-thought (CoT) mechanism to generate both the reasoning chain and the answer, which enhances the model’s capabilities in conducting reasoning. However, due to LLM’s uninterpretable nature and the extreme flexibility of free-form explanations, several challenges remain: such as struggling with inaccurate reasoning, hallucinations, and not aligning with human preferences. In this talk, we will focus on (1) our design of leveraging structured information (that is grounded to the context), for the explainable complex question answering and reasoning; (2) our multi-module interpretable framework for inductive reasoning, which conducts step-wise faithful reasoning with iterative feedback.

papers.title: The Reasoning-Memorization Interplay in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation, and can we identify linear features that mediate this interplay?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies linear reasoning features (LiReFs) in the residual stream of LLMs that mediate the switch between reasoning and memorization, and shows that intervening on these features can improve reasoning performance and generalizability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that linear reasoning features in the residual stream mediate the reasoning-memorization interplay in LLMs, and that targeted intervention on these features can enhance reasoning performance and generalizability, offering insights for more robust and interpretable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Linear Reasoning Features (LiReFs) can be extracted from the residual stream by contrasting reasoning-intensive and memory-intensive questions.
LiReFs separate questions by their required capability (reasoning vs. memory) across domains and languages.
The activation along LiReFs correlates with the reasoning score assigned by GPT-4o, indicating a spectrum from memory to reasoning.
Inference-time intervention on LiReFs (adding or ablating) can improve model performance on both memory and reasoning tasks.
LiReF intervention enhances genuine reasoning generalizability, as shown on GSM-Symbolic, and reduces reasoning errors.
papers.limitation: The study's definition of memorization as poor generalizability may not capture other forms of memorization (e.g., counterfactual memorization).
future_direction: Investigate whether perturbational and counterfactual memorization are mechanistically equivalent and mediated by LiReFs.
Extend the LiReF analysis to more models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on a variety of reasoning benchmarks, but previous studies suggest they sometimes struggle to generalize to unseen questions, potentially due to over-reliance on memorized training examples. However, the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation remain unclear. In this work, we provide a mechanistic understanding of LLMs' reasoning-memorization dynamics by identifying a set of linear features in the model's residual stream that govern the balance between genuine reasoning and memory recall. These features not only distinguish reasoning tasks from memory-intensive ones but can also be manipulated to causally influence model performance on reasoning tasks. Additionally, we show that intervening in these reasoning features helps the model more accurately activate the most relevant problem-solving capabilities during answer generation. Our findings offer new insights into the underlying mechanisms of reasoning and memory in LLMs and pave the way for the development of more robust and interpretable generative AI systems.

papers.title: How does GPT-2 compute greater-than?: Interpreting mathematical abilities in a pre-trained language model
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 compute the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies and explains a circuit in GPT-2 small responsible for computing the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task, showing it activates across diverse contexts.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a detailed circuit-level explanation of a mathematical ability in a pre-trained LM, laying groundwork for future work on memorization and generalization in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A circuit consisting of specific attention heads and MLPs (8-11) is responsible for the greater-than computation.
Attention heads identify the start year YY and communicate it to downstream MLPs.
MLPs 9, 10, and 11 compute the greater-than operation, with MLP 10 playing a central role.
The circuit generalizes to other tasks requiring greater-than but also incorrectly activates in some contexts (e.g., less-than tasks).
The mechanism is more complex than simple memorization but does not reflect full mathematical generalization.
papers.limitation:
Limited by the small size of the model (GPT-2 small) and the simple phenomenon studied.
The study is model-centric; data-driven interpretability techniques would strengthen the work.
future_direction: Studying circuit performance across more diverse tasks to better measure generalization.
Studying larger models to confirm if the results hold.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models can be surprisingly adept at tasks they were not explicitly trained on, but how they implement these capabilities is poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the basic mathematical abilities often acquired by pre-trained language models. Concretely, we use mechanistic interpretability techniques to explain the (limited) mathematical abilities of GPT-2 small. As a case study, we examine its ability to take in sentences such as "The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17", and predict valid two-digit end years (years > 32). We first identify a circuit, a small subset of GPT-2 small's computational graph that computes this task's output. Then, we explain the role of each circuit component, showing that GPT-2 small's final multi-layer perceptrons boost the probability of end years greater than the start year. Finally, we find related tasks that activate our circuit. Our results suggest that GPT-2 small computes greater-than using a complex but general mechanism that activates across diverse contexts.

papers.title: Beyond Words: A Latent Memory Approach to Internal Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can incorporating implicit mental representations (latent memory) into LLMs lead to more efficient internal reasoning compared to explicit chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework that integrates an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into LLMs to enhance internal reasoning efficiency using latent representations, demonstrating reduced training loss compared to a baseline model.
papers.conclusion: The Implicit Memory Module framework improves model efficiency for internal reasoning, and future work can explore integrating explicit interpretability channels without compromising computational gains.
papers.key_findings:
Incorporating the IMM into a GPT model reduced final training loss by 35% to 57% across different context window sizes.
The IMM is designed to be computationally efficient and scalable, with overhead that is minimal compared to standard transformer operations.
The framework allows for optional integration of an explicit chain-of-thought decoder for interpretability without burdening the core inference process.
Preliminary experiments on adaptive long-term memory during inference revealed challenges including increased computational cost, stability issues, and security risks.
papers.limitation:
Preliminary experiments were conducted on a small dataset (Shakespeare) with limited context windows.
Attempts at adaptive long-term memory during inference increased computational costs, introduced stability issues like catastrophic forgetting, and posed potential security risks.
future_direction: Explore safer and more effective methods to incorporate explicit auditability without compromising computational efficiency, such as lightweight chain-of-thought decoders.
Conduct further theoretical analysis and ablation studies, such as varying the number of memory slots and testing different summarization strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have popularized the chain-of-thought (CoT) paradigm, in which models produce explicit reasoning steps in natural language. Although this approach improves interpretability and facilitates external auditing, it may not represent the most computationally efficient method for internal reasoning. In contrast, human cognition relies on implicit mental representations that recall past sensory and episodic information without requiring complete verbalization. In this paper, we propose a framework that integrates implicit mental representations into the internal reasoning processes of LLMs. Preliminary experiments indicate that incorporating an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into a simple GPT model yields a reduction of between 35% and 57% in final training loss compared to a regular GPT baseline. The addition of an explicit interpretability channel (e.g., a chain-of-thought decoder) is straightforward to implement within this approach. We outline theoretical foundations, propose technical mechanisms to scale the memory module, and discuss how these ideas may lead to more efficient and robust reasoning, with optional future extensions for explicit auditability.

papers.title: Dynamic Thinking-Token Selection for Efficient Reasoning in Large Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) excel at solving complex problems by explicitly generating a reasoning trace before deriving the final answer. However, these extended generations incur substantial memory footprint and computational overhead, bottlenecking LRMs' efficiency. This work uses attention maps to analyze the influence of reasoning traces and uncover an interesting phenomenon: only some decision-critical tokens in a reasoning trace steer the model toward the final answer, while the remaining tokens contribute negligibly. Building on this observation, we propose Dynamic Thinking-Token Selection (DynTS). This method identifies decision-critical tokens and retains only their associated Key-Value (KV) cache states during inference, evicting the remaining redundant entries to optimize efficiency.

papers.title: Mind Scramble: Unveiling Large Language Model Psychology Via Typoglycemia
papers.research_question: Does LLM possess human-like cognitive processes and mechanisms in reading and comprehending? The paper uses Typoglycemia to explore this.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LLM Psychology, a framework that uses Typoglycemia experiments to study cognitive behaviors of LLMs. It finds that LLMs exhibit human-like behaviors but are fundamentally data-driven, and each LLM has a unique cognitive pattern.
papers.conclusion: The study advances research on aligning LLMs with human cognition and provides evidence that LLMs' abilities are data-driven, offering a case for LLM Psychology.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as slightly lower task accuracy with consuming more tokens and time.
Different LLMs show varying degrees of robustness to scrambled input, making it a democratized benchmark for model evaluation.
The impact of different task types varies, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) in scrambled format being more challenging.
LLMs' emergent human-like abilities are fundamentally statistical and data-driven, rather than genuinely resembling human cognition.
Each LLM exhibits its unique and consistent 'cognitive pattern' across various tasks, unveiling a general mechanism in its psychology process.
papers.abstract: Research into the external behaviors and internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in addressing complex tasks in the physical world. Studies suggest that powerful LLMs, like GPT-4, are beginning to exhibit human-like cognitive abilities, including planning, reasoning, and reflection. In this paper, we introduce a research line and methodology called LLM Psychology, leveraging human psychology experiments to investigate the cognitive behaviors and mechanisms of LLMs. We migrate the Typoglycemia phenomenon from psychology to explore the "mind" of LLMs. Unlike human brains, which rely on context and word patterns to comprehend scrambled text, LLMs use distinct encoding and decoding processes. Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: Analyzing Chain-of-Thought Prompting in Large Language Models via Gradient-based Feature Attributions
papers.research_question: What is the effect of chain-of-thought prompting on the saliency scores of input tokens in large language models, and does it make model behavior more robust to question perturbations and output variations?
papers.core_contribution: Chain-of-thought prompting does not increase the magnitude of saliency scores for semantically relevant input tokens compared to standard prompting, but it increases the robustness of these scores to question rewordings and stochasticity in model output.
papers.conclusion: Even at model scales where accuracy improvements from CoT prompting do not materialize, its use induces significant changes in saliency scores, highlighting the need for mechanistic investigation. The methodology of using gradient-based feature attribution is an effective step towards characterizing model responsiveness to CoT.
papers.key_findings:
CoT prompting does not improve model accuracy at the 6B parameter scale (except on SST), corroborating prior scale findings.
CoT prompting decreases the absolute magnitude of saliency scores for relevant input tokens across all datasets compared to standard prompting.
CoT prompting makes saliency scores more robust to question rewordings, showing less variation between original and reworded versions.
CoT prompting increases the stability of saliency scores across random model outputs, resulting in lower variance across repeated runs.
The 'dilution' of saliency scores under CoT may be due to longer prompt length and the model spreading attention over more tokens.
papers.limitation:
Limited to models of up to 6B parameters due to computational constraints, so findings may not generalize to larger models where CoT is more effective.
Small dataset size (50 questions per dataset) may limit statistical power and generalizability.
Manual annotation of relevant tokens is subjective and may introduce inconsistency.
future_direction: Repeat the methodology on larger models to examine if findings differ or become more conclusive.
Increase the number of questions and datasets evaluated for greater statistical rigor.
Use more procedural methods (e.g., spaCy) for identifying relevant tokens and crowdsourcing for generating reworded questions.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting has been shown to empirically improve the accuracy of large language models (LLMs) on various question answering tasks. While understanding why CoT prompting is effective is crucial to ensuring that this phenomenon is a consequence of desired model behavior, little work has addressed this; nonetheless, such an understanding is a critical prerequisite for responsible model deployment. We address this question by leveraging gradient-based feature attribution methods which produce saliency scores that capture the influence of input tokens on model output. Specifically, we probe several open-source LLMs to investigate whether CoT prompting affects the relative importances they assign to particular input tokens. Our results indicate that while CoT prompting does not increase the magnitude of saliency scores attributed to semantically relevant tokens in the prompt compared to standard few-shot prompting, it increases the robustness of saliency scores to question perturbations and variations in model output.

papers.title: Are language models aware of the road not taken? Token-level uncertainty and hidden state dynamics
papers.research_question: Do language models represent the alternate paths they could take during generation? How do hidden activations correlate with token-level uncertainty and steering success?
papers.core_contribution: Hidden activations in language models correlate with token-level uncertainty and can be used to steer generation and predict future outcome distributions, indicating that models implicitly represent alternate reasoning paths.
papers.conclusion: Hidden activations in language models reflect token-level uncertainty and can be used to estimate outcome distributions efficiently, offering a way to understand and control model decision-making.
papers.key_findings:
Steering success correlates with token-level uncertainty: models are most steerable when they are least certain about the final answer.
Hidden activations contain information about the model's future outcome distribution, as linear probes on the model's own activations predict outcome distribution better than probes on another model's embeddings.
The dynamics of steering success and outcome distribution are similar, with abrupt changes at the same token positions identified by change point detection.
The correlation between steering success and base outcome probability is moderate (R=0.57) and consistent across examples (average R=0.64).
Linear probes are most predictive in middle layers (layers 6-10) of the model.
papers.limitation:
The computational cost of Forking Paths Analysis is high, requiring millions of tokens to analyze a single base path completion.
Only a handful of examples from three datasets are analyzed due to computational constraints.
papers.abstract: When a language model generates text, the selection of individual tokens might lead it down very different reasoning paths, making uncertainty difficult to quantify. In this work, we consider whether reasoning language models represent the alternate paths that they could take during generation. To test this hypothesis, we use hidden activations to control and predict a language model's uncertainty during chain-of-thought reasoning. In our experiments, we find a clear correlation between how uncertain a model is at different tokens, and how easily the model can be steered by controlling its activations. This suggests that activation interventions are most effective when there are alternate paths available to the model -- in other words, when it has not yet committed to a particular final answer. We also find that hidden activations can predict a model's future outcome distribution, demonstrating that models implicitly represent the space of possible paths.

papers.title: Understanding Reasoning in Chain-of-Thought from the Hopfieldian View
papers.research_question: How does the reasoning capability emerge through Chain-of-Thought prompting? The paper aims to explain the fundamental factors behind CoT's success.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a Hopfieldian view of Chain-of-Thought reasoning, connecting it to cognitive neuroscience, and proposes the Representation-of-Thought framework to enhance robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a Hopfieldian framework for CoT interpretability, introducing error localization and the RoT framework, which improves robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The Hopfieldian view provides a framework to understand CoT reasoning as movement between representation spaces.
A method for localizing reasoning errors in CoT responses is developed based on low-dimensional representation spaces.
The Representation-of-Thought (RoT) framework enhances the robustness of CoT reasoning by manipulating hidden states towards representation spaces.
Experimental results show RoT improves accuracy on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks.
RoT offers fine-grained control over the reasoning process and improves interpretability.
future_direction: Exploring other elements of the Hopfieldian view such as attractors and state space.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated remarkable abilities across various tasks, with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting emerging as a key technique to enhance reasoning capabilities. However, existing research primarily focuses on improving performance, lacking a comprehensive framework to explain and understand the fundamental factors behind CoT's success. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel perspective grounded in the Hopfieldian view of cognition in cognitive neuroscience. We establish a connection between CoT reasoning and key cognitive elements such as stimuli, actions, neural populations, and representation spaces. From our view, we can understand the reasoning process as the movement between these representation spaces. Building on this insight, we develop a method for localizing reasoning errors in the response of CoTs. Moreover, we propose the Representation-of-Thought (RoT) framework, which leverages the robustness of low-dimensional representation spaces to enhance the robustness of the reasoning process in CoTs. Experimental results demonstrate that RoT improves the robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning while offering fine-grained control over the reasoning process.

papers.title: Scaling Competence, Shrinking Reasoning: Cognitive Signatures in Language Model Learning
papers.research_question: How do reasoning tokens evolve during fine-tuning, and can they serve as indicators of learning stages?
papers.core_contribution: Reasoning tokens in language models expand, peak, and contract during fine-tuning, mirroring the Four Stages of Competence, and their dynamics can serve as metrics for diagnosing training stages and guiding early stopping.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning tokens serve as a dynamic scaffold during fine-tuning, providing insights into model learning dynamics and practical tools for diagnosing training progress and optimizing learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning token length increases with performance early in training, peaks at conscious competence, then declines as the model internalizes the task.
Models retain task performance after training even when reasoning tokens are removed, indicating that reasoning scaffolds learning but becomes unnecessary once competence is acquired.
The progression of reasoning tokens aligns with the Four Stages of Competence framework from cognitive science.
Reasoning token dynamics can diagnose training stages, detect convergence, and inform early stopping criteria.
The pattern is consistent across multiple models and tasks including code generation, math problems, and logical question answering.
papers.limitation:
Reasoning token length and correctness are surface-level proxies for internal cognitive processes, and the use of competence stages is interpretive rather than diagnostic.
Experiments are limited to math, logic, and code generation tasks, and may not generalize to tasks with high ambiguity or contextual sensitivity.
The proposed metrics may be less stable in settings with noisy supervision, curriculum learning, or large-scale instruction tuning.
future_direction: Future work may formalize these analogies further or challenge them with deeper mechanistic analysis.
papers.abstract: We analyze reasoning in language models during task-specific fine-tuning and draws parallel between reasoning tokens--intermediate steps generated while solving problem and the human working memory. Drawing from cognitive science, we align training dynamics with the Four Stages of Competence: models initially produce incorrect outputs without reasoning, then begin reasoning (but still fail), eventually reason effectively, and finally solve tasks without explicit reasoning. We find that reasoning token length expands as performance improves, peaks at the stage of conscious competence, then declines as the model internalizes the task. Notably, after training, models retain performance even when reasoning is removed--suggesting it scaffolded learning but is no longer needed. This progression offers actionable insights: reasoning token dynamics can serve as a signal for diagnosing training stage, identifying convergence, and guiding early stopping. We propose metrics to track this trajectory and argue that reasoning behavior is valuable for understanding and optimizing reasoning model training.

papers.title: Disentangling Memory and Reasoning Ability in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we disentangle memory recall and reasoning steps in large language models to improve performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a novel LLM inference paradigm that disentangles memory recall and reasoning steps using special tokens, enhancing both accuracy and interpretability in complex QA tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed decomposition of memory and reasoning steps in LLMs leads to improved performance and greater interpretability, enabling better error analysis and model refinement.
papers.key_findings:
The method improves LLM performance on StrategyQA, CommonsenseQA, and TruthfulQA benchmarks, outperforming baselines like CoT and planning tokens.
On TruthfulQA, the enhanced LLaMA-3.1-8B model achieves 86.6% accuracy, surpassing GPT-4o with CoT prompting.
Error analysis reveals that most errors originate from reasoning steps rather than memory recall, highlighting reasoning as the primary challenge.
The decomposition enhances interpretability by allowing clear separation of memory and reasoning steps in the inference process.
Attention analysis shows that special tokens receive higher attention weights, indicating their role in guiding knowledge and reasoning content generation.
papers.limitation:
Dependency on training data quality for memory recall
Token utilization complexity due to special tokens
Performance may struggle with highly complex reasoning tasks
Computation overhead from decomposing steps
future_direction: Dynamic memory updating to incorporate new information without retraining.
Adaptive reasoning steps based on task complexity.
Interpretable error analysis tools for tracing failures to memory or reasoning steps.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in handling complex tasks requiring both extensive knowledge and reasoning abilities. However, the existing LLM inference pipeline operates as an opaque process without explicit separation between knowledge retrieval and reasoning steps, making the model's decision-making process unclear and disorganized. This ambiguity can lead to issues such as hallucinations and knowledge forgetting, which significantly impact the reliability of LLMs in high-stakes domains. In this paper, we propose a new inference paradigm that decomposes the complex inference process into two distinct and clear actions: (1) memory recall: which retrieves relevant knowledge, and (2) reasoning: which performs logical steps based on the recalled knowledge. To facilitate this decomposition, we introduce two special tokens memory and reason, guiding the model to distinguish between steps that require knowledge retrieval and those that involve reasoning. Our experiment results show that this decomposition not only improves model performance but also enhances the interpretability of the inference process, enabling users to identify sources of error and refine model responses effectively. The code is available at https://github.com/MingyuJ666/Disentangling-Memory-and-Reasoning.

papers.title: Selection-Inference: Exploiting Large Language Models for Interpretable Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can we improve the multi-step logical reasoning capabilities of large language models while producing interpretable, causal reasoning traces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Selection-Inference (SI) framework, which decomposes logical reasoning into iterative selection and inference steps using frozen LLMs, significantly improving performance on multi-step reasoning tasks and producing causal, interpretable reasoning traces.
papers.conclusion: The Selection-Inference framework effectively improves the logical reasoning capabilities of LLMs by breaking down problems into iterative selection and inference steps, yielding both performance gains and interpretable, causal reasoning traces.
papers.key_findings:
Vanilla LLMs perform well on single-step inference but struggle with multi-step logical reasoning.
The SI framework with a 7B LLM almost triples the performance of the same model used naively and outperforms a 40x larger 280B LLM baseline on a suite of logical reasoning tasks.
The SI framework produces causal, natural language reasoning traces that justify the final answer, aiding interpretability and trust.
The modular design of SI allows for error recovery and human inspection of intermediate reasoning steps.
Fine-tuning the Selection and Inference modules on single reasoning steps further improves performance beyond prompt engineering.
papers.limitation:
The main point of failure tends to be the Selection module, which is difficult to quantify without labeled data for intermediate steps.
The approach assumes a database of facts or rules is given, which may not be available in practical settings requiring knowledge retrieval.
The model uses a fixed compute budget (number of steps) and lacks a mechanism for deciding when to halt the reasoning process or filtering reasoning traces.
future_direction: Combine the SI model with knowledge retrieval methods to relax the assumption of given context.
Address the halting problem and develop mechanisms to filter reasoning traces and select the best answer.
Explore fine-tuning the modules for specific tasks to improve performance beyond prompt engineering.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to be capable of impressive few-shot generalisation to new tasks. However, they still tend to perform poorly on multi-step logical reasoning problems. Here we carry out a comprehensive evaluation of LLMs on 50 tasks that probe different aspects of logical reasoning. We show that language models tend to perform fairly well at single step inference or entailment tasks, but struggle to chain together multiple reasoning steps to solve more complex problems. In light of this, we propose a Selection-Inference (SI) framework that exploits pre-trained LLMs as general processing modules, and alternates between selection and inference to generate a series of interpretable, casual reasoning steps leading to the final answer. We show that a 7B parameter LLM used within the SI framework in a 5-shot generalisation setting, with no fine-tuning, yields a performance improvement of over 100% compared to an equivalent vanilla baseline on a suite of 10 logical reasoning tasks. The same model in the same setting even outperforms a significantly larger 280B parameter baseline on the same suite of tasks. Moreover, answers produced by the SI framework are accompanied by a causal natural-language-based reasoning trace, which has important implications for the safety and trustworthiness of the system.

papers.title: Circular Reasoning: Understanding Self-Reinforcing Loops in Large Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: What is the 'Circular Reasoning' failure mode in Large Reasoning Models, and how can we systematically analyze its mechanisms and predict its onset?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies the 'Circular Reasoning' failure mode in Large Reasoning Models, introduces LoopBench for systematic evaluation, analyzes the mechanisms (state collapse, triggers, persistence via V-shaped attention), and proposes an early prediction method using CUSUM on hidden states.
papers.conclusion: Circular reasoning is a critical failure mode in LRMs that stems from intrinsic generation mechanisms, and the proposed analysis and prediction method provide a foundation for improving reasoning stability.
papers.key_findings:
Circular reasoning manifests as two distinct loop types: numerical loops (universal) and statement loops (prevalent in reasoning models).
LoopBench triggers significantly higher repetition rates than existing benchmarks, revealing model fragility.
The loop onset is triggered by reasoning impasses and sustained by a self-reinforcing V-shaped attention pattern.
Early prediction of statement loops is feasible by monitoring hidden state shifts with the CUSUM algorithm.
Decoding strategies mitigate but do not eliminate repetition, indicating an inherent trade-off between loop and accuracy.
papers.limitation:
LoopBench focuses on specific task patterns (high-precision arithmetic and complex recursive reasoning) and may not cover all reasoning scenarios.
The early prediction method is only validated for statement loops, not numerical loops.
The analysis is primarily conducted on open-source models, limiting generalizability to closed-source models.
future_direction: Expand LoopBench to more diverse tasks and domains.
Investigate loop mitigation strategies, such as dynamic decoding or architectural modifications.
Extend the analysis to more model architectures and scales.
papers.abstract: Despite the success of test-time scaling, Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) frequently encounter repetitive loops that lead to computational waste and inference failure. In this paper, we identify a distinct failure mode termed Circular Reasoning. Unlike traditional model degeneration, this phenomenon manifests as a self-reinforcing trap where generated content acts as a logical premise for its own recurrence, compelling the reiteration of preceding text. To systematically analyze this phenomenon, we introduce LoopBench, a dataset designed to capture two distinct loop typologies: numerical loops and statement loops. Mechanistically, we characterize circular reasoning as a state collapse exhibiting distinct boundaries, where semantic repetition precedes textual repetition. We reveal that reasoning impasses trigger the loop onset, which subsequently persists as an inescapable cycle driven by a self-reinforcing V-shaped attention mechanism. Guided by these findings, we employ the Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) algorithm to capture these precursors for early loop prediction. Experiments across diverse LRMs validate its accuracy and elucidate the stability of long-chain reasoning.

papers.title: Understanding and Steering the Cognitive Behaviors of Reasoning Models at Test-Time
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often rely on long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to solve complex tasks. While effective, these trajectories are frequently inefficient, leading to high latency from excessive token generation, or unstable reasoning that alternates between underthinking (shallow, inconsistent steps) and overthinking (repetitive, verbose reasoning). In this work, we study the structure of reasoning trajectories and uncover specialized attention heads that correlate with distinct cognitive behaviors such as verification and backtracking. By lightly intervening on these heads at inference time, we can steer the model away from inefficient modes. Building on this insight, we propose CREST, a training-free method for Cognitive REasoning Steering at Test-time. CREST has two components: (1) an offline calibration step that identifies cognitive heads and derives head-specific steering vectors, and (2) an inference-time procedure that rotates hidden representations to suppress components along those vectors. CREST adaptively suppresses unproductive reasoning behaviors, yielding both higher accuracy and lower computational cost. Across diverse reasoning benchmarks and models, CREST improves accuracy by up to 17.5% while reducing token usage by 37.6%, offering a simple and effective pathway to faster, more reliable LLM reasoning.

papers.title: PlanT: Explainable Planning Transformers via Object-Level Representations
papers.research_question: Is a detailed pixel-level representation necessary for planning in self-driving, or can a compact object-level representation achieve state-of-the-art performance while being more efficient and explainable?
papers.core_contribution: PlanT, a transformer-based planner using a compact object-level representation, achieves state-of-the-art driving performance, is faster than pixel-based baselines, and provides explainability via attention weights.
papers.conclusion: PlanT is an efficient, high-performance, and explainable planner for autonomous driving, demonstrating the effectiveness of object-level representations and transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
PlanT achieves expert-level driving performance on the Longest6 benchmark.
PlanT is 5.3x faster than equivalent pixel-based planning baselines during inference.
An object-level representation is sufficient for planning and outperforms pixel-based representations.
The attention weights of PlanT can reliably identify the most relevant objects in a scene for planning decisions.
PlanT combined with an off-the-shelf perception module outperforms prior sensor-based methods by more than 10 points in driving score.
papers.limitation:
The expert driver used for imitation learning does not achieve a perfect score and has consistent failure modes.
All experiments are conducted in simulation; real-world scenarios are more diverse and challenging.
The perception module used is off-the-shelf and not optimized for PlanT, leading to sub-optimal performance.
future_direction: A thorough analysis of perception robustness and uncertainty encoding.
papers.abstract: Planning an optimal route in a complex environment requires efficient reasoning about the surrounding scene. While human drivers prioritize important objects and ignore details not relevant to the decision, learning-based planners typically extract features from dense, high-dimensional grid representations containing all vehicle and road context information. In this paper, we propose PlanT, a novel approach for planning in the context of self-driving that uses a standard transformer architecture. PlanT is based on imitation learning with a compact object-level input representation. On the Longest6 benchmark for CARLA, PlanT outperforms all prior methods (matching the driving score of the expert) while being 5.3x faster than equivalent pixel-based planning baselines during inference. Combining PlanT with an off-the-shelf perception module provides a sensor-based driving system that is more than 10 points better in terms of driving score than the existing state of the art. Furthermore, we propose an evaluation protocol to quantify the ability of planners to identify relevant objects, providing insights regarding their decision-making. Our results indicate that PlanT can focus on the most relevant object in the scene, even when this object is geometrically distant.

papers.title: Dissociation of Faithful and Unfaithful Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do LLMs recover from errors in Chain of Thought, and what factors affect faithful versus unfaithful recovery?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that LLMs have two distinct modes of reasoning (faithful and unfaithful) when recovering from errors in chain-of-thought, and these modes respond differently to factors like error magnitude and context.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have two distinct reasoning modes: one faithful and interpretable, and one unfaithful where the generated text does not accurately represent the internal reasoning. This challenges the reliability of chain-of-thought for model auditing.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs recover more frequently from larger errors than smaller ones.
Prior expectations of errors (via context noise or prompting) increase error recovery rates.
More evidence for the correct value in the context increases error recovery rates.
Faithful and unfaithful recoveries respond differently to interventions, indicating distinct mechanisms.
Different models (GPT-4, Claude-3 Opus, Llama-3) show varying patterns in faithful vs. unfaithful recovery.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to mathematical reasoning problems and does not investigate non-mathematical reasoning errors; additionally, the introduced errors may differ from naturally occurring errors.
future_direction: Understanding the mechanisms underlying faithful and unfaithful reasoning modes
Identifying factors that influence which reasoning mode is activated
Developing techniques to encourage faithful reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often improve their performance in downstream tasks when they generate Chain of Thought reasoning text before producing an answer. We investigate how LLMs recover from errors in Chain of Thought. Through analysis of error recovery behaviors, we find evidence for unfaithfulness in Chain of Thought, which occurs when models arrive at the correct answer despite invalid reasoning text. We identify factors that shift LLM recovery behavior: LLMs recover more frequently from obvious errors and in contexts that provide more evidence for the correct answer. Critically, these factors have divergent effects on faithful and unfaithful recoveries. Our results indicate that there are distinct mechanisms driving faithful and unfaithful error recoveries. Selective targeting of these mechanisms may be able to drive down the rate of unfaithful reasoning and improve model interpretability.

papers.title: On Memorization of Large Language Models in Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does memorization explain LLMs' performance on reasoning benchmarks, and is memorization only detrimental to learning to reason?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a memorization score (LiMem) and a dynamic K&K benchmark to show that fine-tuned LLMs memorize training puzzles but also improve in generalization, developing reasoning skills alongside memorization.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that memorization and reasoning coexist in fine-tuned LLMs, and the proposed memorization score (LiMem) helps quantify the interplay between them.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can interpolate and memorize training puzzles after fine-tuning, achieving near-perfect accuracy, but struggle with slight variations.
Fine-tuning leads to heavy memorization but also consistently improves generalization performance on K&K puzzles.
LLMs develop reasoning skills on K&K puzzles alongside memorization, as shown by transferability across difficulty levels and probing internal representations.
Fine-tuning with detailed reasoning steps (CoT) can further boost generalization, even when fine-tuned with wrong reasoning steps.
Per-sample memorization score reveals how LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization when solving logical puzzles.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to Knights and Knaves puzzles and may not generalize to other reasoning tasks.
The memorization score LiMem may not capture all forms of memorization.
future_direction: Extend the study to other reasoning tasks beyond K&K puzzles.
Investigate the effect of model scale on memorization and reasoning.
Improve the memorization score to better capture memorization behaviors.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve good performance on challenging reasoning benchmarks, yet could also make basic reasoning mistakes. This contrasting behavior is puzzling when it comes to understanding the mechanisms behind LLMs' reasoning capabilities. One hypothesis is that the increasingly high and nearly saturated performance on common reasoning benchmarks could be due to the memorization of similar problems. In this paper, we systematically investigate this hypothesis with a quantitative measurement of memorization in reasoning tasks, using a dynamically generated logical reasoning benchmark based on Knights and Knaves (K&K) puzzles. We found that LLMs could interpolate the training puzzles (achieving near-perfect accuracy) after fine-tuning, yet fail when those puzzles are slightly perturbed, suggesting that the models heavily rely on memorization to solve those training puzzles. On the other hand, we show that while fine-tuning leads to heavy memorization, it also consistently improves generalization performance. In-depth analyses with perturbation tests, cross difficulty-level transferability, probing model internals, and fine-tuning with wrong answers suggest that the LLMs learn to reason on K&K puzzles despite training data memorization. This phenomenon indicates that LLMs exhibit a complex interplay between memorization and genuine reasoning abilities. Finally, our analysis with per-sample memorization score sheds light on how LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization in solving logical puzzles. Our code and data are available at https://memkklogic.github.io.

papers.title: Factual Probing Is [MASK]: Learning vs. Learning to Recall
papers.research_question: Can we interpret factual probing results as a lower bound on the factual information encoded in a language model, or do prompt-search methods learn from the training data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces OPTI PROMPT, a continuous prompt optimization method that improves factual probing accuracy, and shows that optimized prompts can exploit regularities in training data, complicating the interpretation of probing results.
papers.conclusion: OPTI PROMPT is an effective method for factual probing, but data-driven prompt optimization can exploit training data regularities, making it challenging to interpret probing results as a pure lower bound on model knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
OPTI PROMPT improves top-1 accuracy on the LAMA benchmark by 6.4% over previous methods.
Training data for factual probing contains regularities (e.g., class priors, lexical correlations) that can be exploited by prompt optimization methods.
Optimized prompts can predict facts even when probing randomly initialized models, indicating they learn from training data rather than solely eliciting stored knowledge.
Partitioning test facts into 'easy' (predictable from training data) and 'hard' subsets reveals that OPTI PROMPT improves on both, suggesting it is better at learning from data and eliciting facts from the language model.
Continuous prompt optimization is more efficient and effective than discrete token search, but requires white-box model access.
papers.limitation:
It is difficult to determine whether a prediction comes from the language model's stored knowledge or from patterns learned from the training data during prompt optimization.
Gradient-based prompt optimization methods like OPTI PROMPT require white-box access to the model, limiting their use with API-based large models.
future_direction: Develop techniques for attributing predictions to specific training instances to better understand the source of factual knowledge.
Pursue more mechanistic explanations for how language models learn and represent factual information, beyond prompt-based probing.
papers.abstract: demonstrated that it is possible to retrieve world facts from a pretrained language model by expressing them as cloze-style prompts and interpret the model's prediction accuracy as a lower bound on the amount of factual information it encodes. Subsequent work has attempted to tighten the estimate by searching for better prompts, using a disjoint set of facts as training data. In this work, we make two complementary contributions to better understand these factual probing techniques. First, we propose OPTIPROMPT, a novel and efficient method which directly optimizes in continuous embedding space. We find this simple method is able to predict an additional 6.4% of facts in the LAMA benchmark. Second, we raise a more important question: Can we really interpret these probing results as a lower bound? Is it possible that these prompt-search methods learn from the training data too? We find, somewhat surprisingly, that the training data used by these methods contains certain regularities of the underlying fact distribution, and all the existing prompt methods, including ours, are able to exploit them for better fact prediction. We conduct a set of control experiments to disentangle "learning" from "learning to recall", providing a more detailed picture of what different prompts can reveal about pre-trained language models.

papers.title: Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint
papers.research_question: How do transformers balance global knowledge and in-context learning during training, specifically in the development of induction head mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic bigram dataset and an associative memory viewpoint to study learning dynamics in two-layer transformers, showing that induction heads emerge through top-down gradient-based learning.
papers.conclusion: The associative memory viewpoint provides valuable insights into transformer learning dynamics, offering a foundation for better interpretability and improvements in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Global bigram associations are learned rapidly, while in-context induction mechanisms develop more slowly.
Transformer weight matrices can be viewed as associative memories that store input-output embedding pairs.
The induction head mechanism forms in a top-down manner, with output matrices learning before key-query matrices.
Theoretical gradient analysis shows how associative memories are recovered from noisy inputs during training.
Data distribution properties, such as trigger frequency and output uniformity, affect the learning speed and accuracy of associative memories.
papers.limitation:
The simplified transformer architecture lacks components like non-linear MLPs, multiple heads, and layer normalization, which are present in standard transformers.
The synthetic dataset may not fully capture the complexity of real-world language data.
future_direction: Extending the associative memory viewpoint to non-linear components and multi-head architectures.
Applying insights to optimization algorithms, data selection, and model editing for LLMs.
Studying how such mechanisms scale to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models based on transformers have achieved great empirical successes. However, as they are deployed more widely, there is a growing need to better understand their internal mechanisms in order to make them more reliable. These models appear to store vast amounts of knowledge from their training data, and to adapt quickly to new information provided in their context or prompt. We study how transformers balance these two types of knowledge by considering a synthetic setup where tokens are generated from either global or context-specific bigram distributions. By a careful empirical analysis of the training process on a simplified two-layer transformer, we illustrate the fast learning of global bigrams and the slower development of an "induction head" mechanism for the in-context bigrams. We highlight the role of weight matrices as associative memories, provide theoretical insights on how gradients enable their learning during training, and study the role of data-distributional properties.

papers.title: Causal Abstraction for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Arithmetic Word Problems
papers.research_question: How do chain-of-thought (CoT) prompts improve LLMs' accuracy on arithmetic word problems, and do LLMs actually use their CoTs to reason to their final answers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that CoT-prompted LLMs use their generated chain-of-thought tokens to reason to final answers in arithmetic word problems, as shown through causal abstraction analysis.
papers.conclusion: LLMs achieve higher accuracy with CoT prompting, correct answers correlate with correct CoTs, and LLMs partially realize the causal models from their CoTs, suggesting they use CoTs to reason, though for some LLMs other processes may also play a role.
papers.key_findings:
CoT prompting significantly improves LLM accuracy on the GSM8K test set compared to non-CoT prompting.
Correct final answers are highly correlated with correctly formulated and executed CoTs.
LLMs realize the causal models suggested by their CoTs to a fairly large extent, indicating causal impact of CoT tokens on final answers.
For Cohere Command and PaLM Bison, higher degrees of realization are associated with better overall accuracy.
For OpenAI GPT-3.5, other internal processes may be involved, as shown by intervention-ignoring and self-correcting behavior.
papers.limitation:
Only examines a few LLMs' behavior for a small subset of examples from a single dataset.
Limited to one type of reasoning task (multi-step arithmetic) and may not generalize to other tasks.
Experiments conducted in a controlled setting with temperature 0, so findings may not extend to settings with randomness.
Only found evidence of partial realizations, and the theoretical interpretation of such partial realizations is unclear.
future_direction: Scale up to more examples with more robust human evaluation methods.
Explore cases where LLMs produce incorrect CoTs to examine if they still realize the causal models.
Replicate experiments with LLMs whose internal representations are accessible.
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) achieve higher accuracy on multi-step reasoning tasks when prompted to generate intermediate reasoning steps, or a chain of thought (CoT), before their final answer. However, it is unclear how exactly CoTs improve LLMs’ accuracy, and in particular, if LLMs use their CoTs to reason to their final answers. This paper tries to answer this question with respect to arithmetic word problems, by (i) evaluating the correctness of LLMs’ CoTs, and (ii) using causal abstraction to assess if the intermediate tokens produced as part of a CoT causally impact LLMs’ final answers, in line with the reasoning described by the CoT. We find that for CoT-prompted LLMs, correct answers to arithmetic problems are highly correlated with correct CoTs, and that when LLMs produce correct CoTs, they realize to a fairly large extent the causal models suggested by their CoTs. Higher degrees of realization also seem associated with better overall accuracy on the arithmetic problems. These findings suggest that some CoT-prompted LLMs may do better on multi-step arithmetic reasoning at least partly because they use their CoTs to reason to their final answers. However, for some LLMs, other internal processes may also be involved.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Beyond the Last Answer: Your Reasoning Trace Uncovers More than You Think
papers.research_question: Does the final answer reliably represent the model’s optimal conclusion, and can alternative reasoning paths yield different results?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method to analyze intermediate reasoning steps (subthoughts) in LLM reasoning traces, showing that aggregating answers from subthought completions (mode) improves accuracy and that answer consistency (entropy) correlates with correctness.
papers.conclusion: Evaluating LLMs based solely on the final answer of a reasoning trace can be suboptimal. Analyzing intermediate subthoughts and aggregating answers via mode improves accuracy and provides a signal for reliability.
papers.key_findings:
Selecting the most frequent answer (mode) from completions originating at intermediate subthoughts significantly boosts accuracy compared to relying solely on the final answer of the initial trace.
The distribution of answers generated from subthoughts provides a valuable signal: high consistency (low entropy) correlates with correct baseline solutions, while high fluctuation (high entropy) is characteristic of incorrect solutions.
Non-greedy sampling for subthought completions often yields larger accuracy improvements compared to greedy sampling.
future_direction: Future work could explore integrating these consistency signals into decoding or training.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) leverage step-by-step reasoning to solve complex problems. Standard evaluation practice involves generating a complete reasoning trace and assessing the correctness of the final answer presented at its conclusion. In this paper, we challenge the reliance on the final answer by posing the following two questions: Does the final answer reliably represent the model's optimal conclusion? Can alternative reasoning paths yield different results? To answer these questions, we analyze intermediate reasoning steps, termed subthoughts, and propose a method based on our findings. Our approach involves segmenting a reasoning trace into sequential subthoughts based on linguistic cues. We start by prompting the model to generate continuations from the end-point of each intermediate subthought. We extract a potential answer from every completed continuation originating from different subthoughts. We find that aggregating these answers by selecting the most frequent one (the mode) often yields significantly higher accuracy compared to relying solely on the answer derived from the original complete trace. Analyzing the consistency among the answers derived from different subthoughts reveals characteristics that correlate with the model's confidence and correctness, suggesting potential for identifying less reliable answers. Our experiments across various LLMs and challenging mathematical reasoning datasets (AIME2024 and AIME2025) show consistent accuracy improvements, with gains reaching up to 13\% and 10\% respectively. Implementation is available at: https://github.com/hammoudhasan/SubthoughtReasoner.

papers.title: In-Context Language Learning: Architectures and Algorithms
papers.research_question: Which model classes can perform in-context language learning (ICLL), what algorithmic solutions do they implement, and how can architectural changes improve ICLL?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces in-context language learning (ICLL) as a model problem for studying ICL, shows Transformers outperform other models by implementing n-gram heads, and demonstrates that adding n-gram heads improves ICLL and natural language modeling.
papers.conclusion: ICLL is a useful model problem for understanding ICL, and n-gram heads are a key mechanism in Transformers for ICLL that can be used to improve other models.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers significantly outperform recurrent and convolutional models on ICLL tasks.
Transformers develop specialized n-gram heads (higher-order induction heads) to compute in-context n-gram statistics.
Probing shows that Transformers better encode n-gram counts in hidden states compared to other models.
Hard-wiring n-gram heads into other models (RNNs, convolutional) improves their ICLL performance.
Adding n-gram heads also improves natural language modeling perplexity.
papers.limitation: Many aspects of ICLL, even with regular languages, remain to be understood (e.g. learning dynamics and out-of-distribution generalization).
future_direction: Extend ICLL to more expressive languages (context-free or context-sensitive)
Extend experiments to larger models trained with more tokens
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural language models exhibit a remarkable capacity for in-context learning (ICL): they can infer novel functions from datasets provided as input. Most of our current understanding of when and how ICL arises comes from LMs trained on extremely simple learning problems like linear regression and associative recall. There remains a significant gap between these model problems and the "real" ICL exhibited by LMs trained on large text corpora, which involves not just retrieval and function approximation but free-form generation of language and other structured outputs. In this paper, we study ICL through the lens of a new family of model problems we term in context language learning (ICLL). In ICLL, LMs are presented with a set of strings from a formal language, and must generate additional strings from the same language. We focus on in-context learning of regular languages generated by random finite automata. We evaluate a diverse set of neural sequence models (including several RNNs, Transformers, and state-space model variants) on regular ICLL tasks, aiming to answer three questions: (1) Which model classes are empirically capable of ICLL? (2) What algorithmic solutions do successful models implement to perform ICLL? (3) What architectural changes can improve ICLL in less performant models? We first show that Transformers significantly outperform neural sequence models with recurrent or convolutional representations on ICLL tasks. Next, we provide evidence that their ability to do so relies on specialized "n-gram heads" (higher-order variants of induction heads) that compute input-conditional next-token distributions. Finally, we show that hard-wiring these heads into neural models improves performance not just on ICLL, but natural language modeling -- improving the perplexity of 340M-parameter models by up to 1.14 points (6.7%) on the SlimPajama dataset.

papers.title: Understanding Chain-of-Thought in LLMs through Information Theory
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate the quality of each step in a model's Chain-of-Thought reasoning without requiring annotated step-by-step data, in order to identify failure modes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an information-theoretic framework to quantify the 'information-gain' at each step of a Chain-of-Thought reasoning process, enabling the identification of reasoning failures without the need for expensive annotated step-by-step data.
papers.conclusion: The information-theoretic framework provides a rigorous and practical method for evaluating Chain-of-Thought reasoning in LLMs, enabling granular failure detection without the need for costly annotated data.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Information-Gain method accurately identifies incorrect reasoning steps in Chain-of-Thought, outperforming baseline methods like Outcome Reward Modeling and Math-Shepherd.
The method is effective in detecting errors even when the correctness of a step depends on previous steps, a scenario where baselines fail.
It does not require annotated Chain-of-Thought data, making it more scalable than process-based supervision methods.
The framework is validated on synthetic data, GSM8K, and PRM800k datasets, showing consistent performance across different complexities.
The information-gain metric can be applied to both linear and exploratory (e.g., O1/R1-style) reasoning patterns.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance in complex reasoning tasks through the use of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, allowing models to break down problems into manageable sub-tasks. However, existing CoT evaluation techniques either require annotated CoT data or fall short in accurately assessing intermediate reasoning steps, leading to high rates of false positives. In this paper, we formalize CoT reasoning in LLMs through an information-theoretic lens. Specifically, our framework quantifies the `information-gain' at each reasoning step, enabling the identification of failure modes in LLMs without the need for expensive annotated datasets. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through extensive experiments on toy arithmetic, GSM8K and PRM800k datasets, where it significantly outperforms existing outcome-based methods by providing more accurate insights into model performance on individual subtasks.

papers.title: How Chain-of-Thought Works? Tracing Information Flow from Decoding, Projection, and Activation
papers.research_question: How does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting alter a model's internal states to improve reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: CoT works by constraining the decoding space via answer templates, with structural adherence strongly correlating with performance, and modulates neuron activation in a task-dependent manner (reducing activation in open-domain tasks, increasing it in closed-domain tasks).
papers.conclusion: The findings provide a novel mechanistic interpretability framework and critical insights for designing more efficient and robust CoT prompts.
papers.key_findings:
CoT prompts models to imitate structural keywords (e.g., 'time', 'action') from the prompt and content keywords (e.g., numbers) from the input question.
There is a strong positive correlation between adherence to the CoT reasoning structure (measured by Imitation Count) and task performance (accuracy).
CoT leads to more concentrated probability distributions (lower entropy) and higher confidence in generated tokens compared to standard prompting.
CoT reduces the average number of activated neurons in Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) for open-domain tasks, but increases it for closed-domain tasks, indicating task-dependent modulation of neural engagement.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting significantly enhances model reasoning, yet its internal mechanisms remain poorly understood. We analyze CoT's operational principles by reversely tracing information flow across decoding, projection, and activation phases. Our quantitative analysis suggests that CoT may serve as a decoding space pruner, leveraging answer templates to guide output generation, with higher template adherence strongly correlating with improved performance. Furthermore, we surprisingly find that CoT modulates neuron engagement in a task-dependent manner: reducing neuron activation in open-domain tasks, yet increasing it in closed-domain scenarios. These findings offer a novel mechanistic interpretability framework and critical insights for enabling targeted CoT interventions to design more efficient and robust prompts. We released our code and data at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/cot-D247.

papers.title: Lost at the Beginning of Reasoning
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have significantly advanced complex reasoning capabilities, particularly through extended chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning that incorporates mechanisms such as backtracking, self-reflection, and self-correction. Despite these developments, the self-correction abilities of LLMs during long CoT reasoning remain underexplored. And recent findings on overthinking suggest that such models often engage in unnecessarily redundant reasoning. In this work, we empirically show that the first reasoning step exerts a disproportionately large influence on the final prediction. I.e., errors introduced at this stage can substantially degrade subsequent reasoning quality. This phenomenon is consistently observed across various state-of-the-art open- and closed-source reasoning models. Leveraging this insight, we propose an efficient sampling strategy that leverages a reward model to identify and retain high-quality first reasoning steps while discarding suboptimal ones, achieving up to a 70% reduction in inference cost without sacrificing any accuracy. Our work highlights the central role of the first reasoning step in generating a high-quality reasoning trajectory, and thus enabling significantly efficient sampling.

papers.title: Unveiling Internal Reasoning Modes in LLMs: A Deep Dive into Latent Reasoning vs. Factual Shortcuts with Attribute Rate Ratio
papers.research_question: How do latent reasoning and factual shortcuts differ during inference in LLMs for multi-hop questions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Attribute Rate Ratio (ARR) metric to efficiently distinguish between latent reasoning and factual shortcuts in LLMs, and provides an analysis of internal mechanisms showing that latent reasoning encodes bridge-related information while factual shortcuts bypass intermediate steps.
papers.conclusion: The work systematically investigates distinctions between latent reasoning and factual shortcuts, proposes the ARR metric for efficient classification, and demonstrates its application in RAG conflict scenarios, deepening understanding of model reasoning pathways.
papers.key_findings:
Subject representations differ significantly between reasoning modes: latent reasoning encodes bridge-related information for final answer extraction, while factual shortcuts bypass intermediate reasoning and resemble single-hop factual queries.
The proposed Attribute Rate Ratio (ARR) achieves around 90% accuracy in classifying reasoning modes on constructed datasets.
Model behavior under conflicting prompts in RAG scenarios is closely tied to its underlying reasoning mode, with latent reasoning more influenced by external context and factual shortcuts more robust to disruptive information.
The model undergoes two disjointed stages during multi-hop reasoning: local shallow reasoning (encoding relation-related attributes) and deep reasoning (integrating information for final answer).
Bridge-related information propagated from the subject position plays a decisive role in second-hop reasoning for latent reasoning modes.
papers.limitation:
Scope limited to two-hop reasoning, which may not generalize to more complex reasoning chains.
Limited dataset availability for studying latent reasoning due to many shortcut mappings in training data.
Latent multi-hop reasoning pathway identification relies on CoT filtering, which may not fully correspond to the model's internal reasoning processes.
The proposed metric lacks rigorous verification due to model complexity and limited datasets.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex reasoning beyond two-hop tasks.
Further refinement and verification of the ARR metric.
Investigating the balance between external information utilization and robustness in RAG conflicts.
papers.abstract: Yiran Yang, Haifeng Sun, Jingyu Wang, Qi Qi, Zirui Zhuang, Huazheng Wang, Pengfei Ren, Jing Wang, Jianxin Liao. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2025.

papers.title: Mechanistic Unveiling of Transformer Circuits: Self-Influence as a Key to Model Reasoning
papers.research_question: What multi-step reasoning mechanisms are used by language models to solve tasks?
papers.core_contribution: We propose the Self-Influence Circuit Analysis Framework (SICAF) to trace and analyze the thought processes of language models during complex reasoning tasks by combining circuit analysis and self-influence functions.
papers.conclusion: The SICAF framework successfully maps hierarchical reasoning pathways in GPT-2 for the IOI task, revealing a human-like reasoning structure and enhancing model interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed SICAF framework can trace and analyze the thought processes of LMs in complex reasoning tasks.
Circuits identified for the IOI task are small (1-2% of edges) and faithful (recover ≥85% of model performance).
EAP-IG and EAP-IG-KL outperform EAP in normalized faithfulness and converge with fewer parameters.
The model's key parameters for the IOI task are concentrated in the first and last few layers.
The model follows a hierarchical reasoning path: identifying entities in early layers, interpreting actions in middle layers, and synthesizing information in final layers.
papers.limitation:
The analysis was conducted primarily on the GPT-2 model and may not generalize to larger or different architectures without adaptation.
Calculating self-influence requires computationally intensive methods, which may pose scalability challenges for more complex models.
The work focused on a single task (Indirect Object Identification, or IOI), and the applicability of these findings to other natural language processing tasks remains an open question.
future_direction: Explore the adaptability of the approach across varied tasks and model architectures.
Investigate methods to optimize computational efficiency of self-influence calculation.
